tool.name: FastAPI
tool.tagline: Fast, type-hint driven Python framework for building HTTP APIs
tool.description: FastAPI is a modern Python web framework for building APIs, built on Starlette for the web layer and Pydantic for data validation. You declare endpoints as typed functions and get request parsing, validation, JSON serialization and interactive OpenAPI docs from the same code. It is one of the most popular choices for Python back ends, microservices and ML model serving.

glossary.def: The small async web toolkit FastAPI is built on; it handles URL matching, requests, responses, middleware and WebSockets.
The Python library FastAPI uses to check incoming data against your type hints and to turn Python objects into JSON.
The server program that runs a FastAPI app: it listens for HTTP requests on a port and hands each one to your app.
The standard contract between Python async web apps and the servers that run them; FastAPI apps speak it, and Uvicorn runs them.
The fastapi command: 'fastapi dev main.py' runs your app for development with auto-reload; 'fastapi run' runs it for production. Both start Uvicorn for you.
In FastAPI, one URL path plus one HTTP method (such as GET /items) and the Python function that handles it, declared with @app.get, @app.post and so on.
A standard JSON format for describing a web API: its URLs, methods, parameters and data shapes. FastAPI writes one for your app automatically.
The interactive documentation page FastAPI serves at /docs: it lists every operation and lets you fill in parameters and send real requests from the browser.
The read-only API reference page FastAPI serves at /redoc, built from the same OpenAPI schema as /docs.
A changing part of the URL path, written as {item_id} in a FastAPI route, that is captured and passed to your function as an argument.
A name=value pair after the ? in a URL, such as ?skip=0&limit=10; in FastAPI, any function parameter that isn't in the path becomes one.
The status code FastAPI returns when a request's data doesn't match what the function declared, with a JSON body listing each problem.
A class that subclasses pydantic.BaseModel and lists fields with type hints; FastAPI uses it to describe, check and convert JSON data.
The type FastAPI uses to shape and check what a path operation sends back, taken from the function's return annotation or the response_model argument.
typing.Annotated[type, extra...]: a type hint that carries extra information. FastAPI reads the extras, such as Query(max_length=50), to know where a value comes from and which rules it must obey.
A method on a Pydantic model, marked @field_validator or @model_validator, that checks a value with your own code and raises ValueError when it is wrong.
The exception you raise in FastAPI to end a request with an error status, as in raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Not found").
In FastAPI, a function registered with @app.exception_handler(SomeError) that turns that kind of exception, raised anywhere during a request, into a response.

In FastAPI, a function (or class) whose result a path operation needs, declared with Depends(); FastAPI calls it for each request and passes in the result. (In packaging, a dependency is a library your project needs.)
A dependency that another dependency declares with Depends(); FastAPI resolves the whole chain before calling your function.
app.dependency_overrides[real] = fake: a FastAPI dict that swaps one dependency for another, usually so tests can replace a database or login check.
A FastAPI object with the same .get/.post decorators as the app, used to group the path operations of one feature in its own module; the app attaches it with include_router.
A separate Pydantic package whose BaseSettings class reads a typed Settings object from environment variables and .env files, checking the values as it loads them.
A Pydantic type for passwords and keys that prints as ********** in logs and error messages; call .get_secret_value() to read the real value.
A library by FastAPI's author where one class is both a Pydantic model and a database table definition (built on SQLAlchemy), so one declaration gives validation and storage.
The most widely used Python library for working with SQL databases: it builds queries in Python and can map tables to classes.
In SQLAlchemy and SQLModel, the object created once with create_engine(url) that knows how to reach your database and keeps a pool of open connections ready.
In SQLAlchemy and SQLModel, the object that tracks the rows you load and change and sends the changes to the database in one transaction when you commit; FastAPI apps open one per request.
The migration tool for SQLAlchemy: it writes and applies files that change an existing database's tables when your models change.
The simple log-in pattern FastAPI's docs use: the caller posts a username and password to /token, gets a token back, and sends that token with every later request.
A token sent in the Authorization header as 'Bearer <token>'; whoever holds (bears) it is treated as the user it was issued to.
One named piece of information inside a JWT, such as sub (the user id) or exp (when the token expires).
An OPTIONS request a browser sends on its own before a cross-origin request with a JSON body or custom headers, to ask the API whether the real request is allowed.
In the browser's security rules, a site identified by scheme, host and port, such as https://app.example.com. A request from a page to a different origin is cross-origin.
A FastAPI parameter type for small jobs that should run right after the response has been sent, in the same process, such as sending a notification email.
FastAPI's test helper: a pretend HTTP client that sends requests straight into your app, without a server or network, and returns the responses for checking.
In FastAPI, the function that runs once when the app starts (code before its yield) and once when it shuts down (code after), for setting up and closing shared resources.
In FastAPI, the group of 40 threads (per worker, by default) where plain def functions and dependencies run, so a slow call ties up one thread instead of the whole event loop.
A FastAPI dependency written with yield: code before yield sets something up, the yielded value is passed in, and code after yield cleans up once the request is done.
The scope argument of Depends() for yield dependencies: "request" (default) cleans up after the response is sent, "function" right after the path operation function returns.
The dict a FastAPI lifespan function yields; each request can read its entries as request.state.<name>.
The FastAPI parameter type for an uploaded file: it gives the file name, type and size, and keeps big files in a temporary file on disk instead of in memory.
A FastAPI response that sends whatever a generator yields, piece by piece, as it is produced, instead of building the whole body first.
The request body format browsers use for forms with file uploads: the body is split into parts, one per form field or file.
A connection that starts as an HTTP request and then stays open, so server and client can both send messages at any time; used for chat and live updates.
The exception FastAPI raises inside a WebSocket function when the other side has closed the connection.
Publish/subscribe: a messaging pattern where senders publish messages to a named channel and every program subscribed to it receives a copy; Redis offers it.
The unique name OpenAPI gives each path operation; tools that generate client libraries turn it into a method name.
A system that runs many copies of containerized apps across a group of machines, restarting failed copies and spreading traffic between them.
A URL prefix (such as /api) that a proxy adds in front of your app; telling FastAPI about it makes the docs and generated URLs include it.
The part of Pydantic v2 written in Rust, a fast compiled language; it does the actual checking and JSON conversion that your models describe.
A Pydantic object that checks and converts data for any type (such as list[Item]), not just a model class; building one is costly, so create it once.
A Pydantic union of models (Cat | Dog) plus a tag field such as kind, so Pydantic reads the tag and checks against the one matching model instead of trying each.
An open standard and set of libraries for collecting traces, metrics and logs from programs and sending them to monitoring tools.
How many different label combinations a metric has; each one is stored as its own series, so labels like raw user ids can make it explode.

concepts.name: What FastAPI is and your first app
concepts.summary: Install FastAPI, write a five-line app and serve JSON over HTTP with the fastapi dev command.
concepts.why: Everything else in FastAPI builds on this loop: write a function, decorate it, run the server, call the URL.
concepts.body:
When a program needs something from another program on a different computer, it sends a **request** over the network and gets a **response** back. The rules for that exchange on the web are called **HTTP**. Your web **browser** (Chrome, Safari) does this to fetch pages; a mobile app does it to load your messages. Each request goes to a **URL**, an address such as `http://127.0.0.1:8000/items`, and the program that waits for requests and answers them is a **server**.

A server that answers programs rather than people, usually with data in JSON, is a **web API** (an **API** is any agreed way for one program to use another). FastAPI is a Python **web framework** for building them: a library that handles the HTTP plumbing so you write only the functions that do the work.

What makes FastAPI special is that it reads your type hints. From one plain function declaration it checks incoming data, converts your return values to JSON and writes documentation. It stands on two libraries: **Starlette** does the web part (matching URLs, requests, responses) and **Pydantic** checks and converts data.

FastAPI doesn't listen on the network by itself; a server program called **Uvicorn** does that and hands each request to your app. Install both in a virtual environment with the `standard` extras, which bring Uvicorn, the `fastapi` command and common optional packages:

```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install "fastapi[standard]"
```

Save the example as `main.py` and run `fastapi dev main.py` (plain `fastapi dev` also finds a `main.py` with an `app` in it). It starts a server on `http://127.0.0.1:8000`: `127.0.0.1` means "this computer", and 8000 is the **port**, a numbered door the server listens at. The server watches your files and restarts on every save. Open the address in a browser and you get `{"message":"Hello World"}`.

That is a **development server**, for you while you build; restarting on save is called **auto-reload**. The live copy real users rely on is **production**; for it use `fastapi run main.py`: no auto-reload, and it listens on `0.0.0.0`, meaning "reachable from other machines" rather than only your own. Older tutorials show the equivalent `uvicorn main:app --reload`, where `main:app` means "the object `app` in module `main`".

Three things to notice in the code. `app = FastAPI()` creates the application object. `@app.get("/")` registers the function below it to answer GET requests (the kind a browser sends when you open a page) for the path `/`. And returning a `dict` is enough: FastAPI turns it into a JSON response.
takeaways: FastAPI = Starlette for the web layer + Pydantic for data, driven by your type hints
pip install "fastapi[standard]" gives you Uvicorn and the fastapi command
fastapi dev for development (auto-reload), fastapi run for production
Returning a dict, list or model produces a JSON response
pitfalls: Naming your own file fastapi.py: it shadows the real package and the import fails.
Running fastapi dev (auto-reload, reachable only from your own computer) in production.

quiz.q: Which library does FastAPI rely on to validate request data and serialize responses?
quiz.explain: Pydantic checks and converts data; Starlette handles the HTTP layer and Uvicorn is the server.

quiz.q: Compared with fastapi dev, what does fastapi run main.py change?
options: It runs the app without Uvicorn
It turns off auto-reload and listens on 0.0.0.0
It enables auto-reload and is reachable only from your own computer
quiz.explain: fastapi run is the production mode: no file watching, and it accepts connections from other machines.

concepts.name: Path operations and HTTP methods
concepts.summary: Map URL paths and HTTP methods to Python functions with @app.get, @app.post and the other method decorators.
concepts.why: Path operations are the building block of every FastAPI app, and choosing the right method and path is basic API design.
concepts.body:
Every HTTP request names a path and a method. The **path** is the part of the URL after the server's address: in `http://127.0.0.1:8000/items/5` it is `/items/5`. The **HTTP method** is a verb saying what the request wants to do: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`.

FastAPI calls the pair a **path operation**, handled by a *path operation function*. You declare one with a decorator named after the method: `@app.get`, `@app.post`, `@app.put`, `@app.patch`, `@app.delete` (plus the rarer `head`, `options` and `trace`).

Use each method for its agreed meaning, because browsers, other programs and the equipment between them rely on it:

- GET reads and must not change anything. Because it's harmless, a browser may send it again on its own, or keep the answer and reuse it.
- POST creates something or starts an action.
- PUT replaces a thing entirely; PATCH changes part of it.
- DELETE removes it.

One path can have several operations: `GET /items` lists, `POST /items` creates. If no path matches, the caller gets **status code** 404 ("not found"); a status code is the three-digit number in every response saying how it went. If the path exists but not for that method, the answer is 405 ("method not allowed").

Paths are checked **in the order you declare them**. That matters when a fixed path like `/users/me` overlaps a variable one like `/users/{user_id}` (the next lessons cover these): declare the fixed one first.

The function may be `def` or `async def`. Start with plain `def`; FastAPI runs it on a separate thread, so one slow function doesn't hold up the others (the async lesson explains when to switch). Whatever you return (a dict, list, string or number) is converted to JSON.

Decorator arguments configure the operation: `status_code=201` ("created"), `tags=["items"]` to group it in the docs, `summary=...`, `deprecated=True`. The function's docstring becomes its description in the documentation.

The example uses `TestClient`, which sends requests to the app inside the same Python program, with no server; the testing lesson covers it properly.
concepts.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()
items = ["apple", "pear"]

@app.get("/items", tags=["items"])
def list_items():
    """Return every item."""
    return items

@app.post("/items", status_code=201, tags=["items"])
def add_item():
    items.append("plum")
    return {"count": len(items)}

client = TestClient(app)
print(client.get("/items").json())         # ['apple', 'pear']
print(client.post("/items").status_code)   # 201
print(client.put("/items").status_code)    # 405: no PUT for /items
print(client.get("/nope").status_code)     # 404
takeaways: A path operation = path + HTTP method + the function that handles it
Use GET for reads only; POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE for changes
Paths match in declaration order: put fixed paths before variable ones
Unknown path gives 404, known path with the wrong method gives 405
pitfalls: Changing data in a GET function: browsers and automated tools may send GET requests you never asked for, and each one will make the change.

quiz.q: A client sends PUT /items, but only GET and POST are declared for /items. What status code comes back?
quiz.explain: The path exists but not for that method, so FastAPI answers 405.

quiz.q: You declared @app.get('/users/{user_id}') before @app.get('/users/me'), with user_id: int. What happens on GET /users/me?
options: The first route matches and 'me' fails the int check, giving a 422
The /users/me function runs because exact matches always win
FastAPI refuses to start because the routes overlap
quiz.explain: Paths are tried in order, so /users/{user_id} captures 'me' first; declare /users/me before it.

concepts.name: Interactive API docs: /docs and /redoc
concepts.summary: Every app serves an OpenAPI description of itself plus Swagger UI and ReDoc pages, generated from your code.
concepts.why: You get accurate, always up-to-date documentation and a test console for free, for you, your teammates and anyone calling your API.
concepts.body:
Anyone who calls your API needs to know which paths exist, what each expects and what it returns. FastAPI writes that description for you, in **OpenAPI**: the standard JSON format for describing web APIs. It is built from the path operations, parameters, models and type hints you declare, and three URLs expose it out of the box:

- `/docs`: **Swagger UI**, an interactive page where you expand an operation, fill in its parameters and press "Try it out" to send a real request.
- `/redoc`: **ReDoc**, a clean read-only reference.
- `/openapi.json`: the raw description the two pages are built from.

Because the docs are generated from the same declarations FastAPI uses to check requests, they can't fall out of date: add a parameter or change a model field and the docs change on the next reload.

The description is useful beyond the browser. Tools such as openapi-generator or openapi-ts read `/openapi.json` and write a ready-made **client library** (functions that wrap your API) in another language (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift...), so callers don't hand-write requests. Teams also compare the file between releases to spot changes that would break existing callers.

Enrich it cheaply as you go:

- pass `title`, `version` and `description` to `FastAPI(...)` (the description may use Markdown, the simple text formatting with `**bold**` and `# headings`),
- group operations with `tags=[...]`,
- write docstrings, or pass `summary` and `description` to the decorator,
- describe model fields; their descriptions and examples appear in the docs.

To move or remove the pages, pass `docs_url`, `redoc_url` or `openapi_url` to `FastAPI()`; `None` disables one. `openapi_url=None` disables all three, since the pages load the description from it. Some teams switch the docs off in production, but hiding them isn't security: the paths still answer anyone who guesses them, so protect them properly (the Authentication lesson).
concepts.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI(
    title="Inventory API",
    version="1.2.0",
    description="Manage **items** in the warehouse.",
)

@app.get("/items", tags=["items"], summary="List items")
def list_items():
    """Returns all items, newest first."""
    return []

schema = TestClient(app).get("/openapi.json").json()
print(schema["info"]["title"])     # Inventory API
print(list(schema["paths"]))       # ['/items']
print(schema["paths"]["/items"]["get"]["description"])
# Returns all items, newest first.

# With `fastapi dev` running, open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs and /redoc
takeaways: /docs (Swagger UI), /redoc (ReDoc) and /openapi.json come for free
Docs are generated from the same declarations used for checking requests, so they stay accurate
Titles, tags, summaries, docstrings and field descriptions all flow into the docs
docs_url, redoc_url and openapi_url move or disable the pages
pitfalls: Treating disabled docs as protection: the paths still answer requests from anyone.

quiz.q: Why do FastAPI's docs stay in sync with the code?
options: FastAPI compares the docs to the code at startup and warns on drift
An automated step regenerates them on each commit
They're generated while the app runs, from the same type hints and models used for checking requests
Swagger UI scans your source files
quiz.explain: There is only one source of truth: the declarations that also drive reading and checking requests.

quiz.q: You create the app with FastAPI(openapi_url=None). What happens?
options: Only /openapi.json disappears; /docs keeps working from a cached copy
quiz.explain: The pages need the description, so removing its URL disables all three.

concepts.name: Path parameters
concepts.summary: Capture parts of the URL like /items/{item_id} as typed function arguments that FastAPI converts and checks for you.
concepts.why: URLs that name one thing, such as /users/42, are the backbone of most APIs, and typed parameters make them safe to use.
concepts.body:
Many URLs name one particular thing: `/users/42`, `/items/apple`. The changing part is a **path parameter**. Put a name in braces in the path and give the function a parameter with the same name: `@app.get("/items/{item_id}")` with `def read_item(item_id: int)`. FastAPI cuts that piece out of the URL, and the **type hint** decides what happens next:

- For `/items/42`, the text `"42"` is converted, so `item_id` is the int `42`.
- For `/items/abc`, conversion fails and the caller gets a **422** response ("unprocessable content") whose JSON body says which parameter was wrong and why. Your function never runs.

Checking that incoming data has the right shape and values before using it is called **validation**. This is the central FastAPI idea: the type hint is documentation, conversion and validation in one. `int`, `float`, `str`, `bool`, `UUID`, `date` and `datetime` all work out of the box.

When only a fixed set of values is valid, use an `Enum` class that also subclasses `str` (as in the code). FastAPI accepts only its members, the docs show a drop-down, and your function receives the enum member, so compare with `Color.red` or read `.value`.

Path parameters are always required: a URL either has the piece or it matches a different path. A piece can't contain `/`, unless you add `:path`, as in `{file_path:path}`, which matches the rest of the URL including slashes.

Two practical notes. First, path order: with `/users/me` and `/users/{user_id}`, declare `/users/me` first, or `me` is captured as a user id. Second, Pydantic's conversion is relaxed where no information is lost (`"007"` becomes `7`) but strict where some would be: `"3.5"` is rejected for an `int` rather than rounded down.
takeaways: {name} in the path + a parameter with the same name = path parameter
The type hint converts the value; invalid input gets a 422 before your code runs
Use a str Enum to restrict a parameter to fixed values
{name:path} captures the rest of the URL including slashes
pitfalls: Declaring /users/{user_id} before /users/me, so 'me' never reaches its own function.

quiz.q: With def read_item(item_id: int), what does GET /items/007 pass as item_id?
options: Nothing: a 422 because of the leading zeros
quiz.explain: The URL piece is text, and Pydantic converts '007' to the int 7.

quiz.q: What does GET /items/3.5 return for item_id: int?
quiz.explain: Pydantic refuses to drop the fractional part, so the request fails validation.

concepts.name: Query parameters
concepts.summary: Function parameters that aren't in the path become query parameters like ?skip=0&limit=10: typed, optional or required.
concepts.why: Filtering, paging through results, sorting and search options all travel as query parameters.
concepts.body:
A URL can carry extra settings after a `?`, as `name=value` pairs separated by `&`: `/items?skip=0&limit=10`. That part is the **query string**, and each pair is a **query parameter**.

In FastAPI, any function parameter that isn't in the path and has a simple type (int, str, bool, float, enum...) is read from the query string. Types work exactly as for path parameters: values arrive as text and are converted and checked.

Whether a query parameter is required depends only on its default:

- `limit: int = 10` is optional; when it's missing you get 10.
- `q: str | None = None` is optional; when it's missing you get `None`, so test with `if q is not None`.
- `status: str` with no default is required; leaving it out gives a 422.

Booleans are deliberately forgiving: `true`, `1`, `yes` and `on` mean True; `false`, `0`, `no` and `off` mean False (in any letter case). Anything else is a 422.

Path and query parameters mix freely, and the order of the function's parameters doesn't matter: FastAPI identifies each one by name. A name that appears in braces in the path is a path parameter; any other simple-typed parameter is a query parameter.

Lists are the one surprise. To accept a repeated key such as `?tag=a&tag=b`, write `tag: Annotated[list[str], Query()] = []`. Without `Query()`, FastAPI would assume a list parameter is part of the request body (the next lesson). `Query()` also adds rules like `max_length`, which the validation lesson covers.

Use query parameters for things that select or shape a response (filters, paging, sort order), not for data you're creating; that belongs in the request body.
takeaways: Simple-typed parameters not in the path come from the query string
No default = required; a default (often None) = optional
bool accepts true/false, 1/0, yes/no, on/off
Repeated keys need Annotated[list[str], Query()]
pitfalls: Writing q: str = None: it works but lies about the type; use str | None = None.

quiz.q: For def search(q: str, page: int = 1), what does GET /search?page=2 return?
options: Results with q set to None
A 422 error because q is required
quiz.explain: q has no default, so it's a required query parameter and its absence fails validation.

quiz.q: GET /items?active=off reaches active: bool = True. What value does active have?
options: True, because any non-empty string is truthy
quiz.explain: FastAPI's bool conversion understands off/no/0/false as False.

concepts.name: Request bodies with Pydantic models
concepts.summary: Declare a Pydantic BaseModel parameter and FastAPI reads the JSON request body, checks it and turns it into an object.
concepts.why: Creating and updating things means accepting structured JSON safely, and models let you describe the shape once.
concepts.body:
Path and query parameters carry a few small values. When a caller sends a whole record, such as a new item to create, it goes in the **request body**: the main content of the request, after its first lines, usually as JSON.

To accept a JSON body in a POST, PUT or PATCH, describe its shape as a **Pydantic model**: a class inheriting from `BaseModel` whose annotated attributes are its fields. Use the model as a parameter type and FastAPI reads the body as JSON, **parses** it (turns the text into Python values), checks types and required fields (nested models too), and hands your function a model instance with attributes like `item.price`. The docs describe the expected JSON as well.

So FastAPI decides where each parameter comes from like this: names in the path are path parameters, simple types are query parameters, Pydantic models are the body. Model fields follow the familiar default rules: no default means required, `str | None = None` means optional.

By default Pydantic converts input where it safely can, so the JSON text `"3"` for an `int` field becomes 3, and rejects what can't be converted, such as `"abc"` for a float. Failures produce a 422 whose `detail` is a list of errors; each has a `loc` such as `["body", "price"]`, a `msg` and a `type`, so callers can point at the exact field. Extra keys the model doesn't define are ignored by default; set `model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")` to reject them instead.

Models nest naturally: a field can be another model, `list[Tag]` or `dict[str, int]`. To get plain data back out, use `item.model_dump()` (a dict) or `item.model_dump_json()`. The older names `.dict()` and `.json()` still work but are **deprecated**: officially discouraged and due for removal. For partial updates, `item.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)` returns only the fields the caller actually sent.

If a function has two model parameters, FastAPI expects a JSON object with one key per parameter name: `{"item": {...}, "user": {...}}`.
takeaways: A BaseModel parameter = JSON request body, checked and parsed
Path names are path parameters, simple types are query parameters, models are the body
Validation errors are 422s with a precise loc for each failing field
Use model_dump() / model_dump_json(), not the deprecated .dict() / .json()
pitfalls: Sending form fields or query parameters when the function expects JSON: the body must be JSON.

quiz.q: In def update(item_id: int, item: Item, q: str | None = None), where does FastAPI read item from?
quiz.explain: Pydantic model parameters are read from the request body.

quiz.q: A client sends {"name": "Pen", "price": 2, "color": "red"} to a model with only name and price. What happens by default?
options: color is added to the instance as an extra attribute
quiz.explain: Pydantic ignores unknown keys by default; extra="forbid" turns them into errors.

concepts.name: Response models and status codes
concepts.summary: Use return type annotations or response_model to shape, filter and document what a path operation sends back.
concepts.why: Response models stop you from leaking fields like password hashes and give callers a documented, stable contract.
concepts.body:
FastAPI checks what comes in, and a **response model** controls what goes out. The simplest way is a return type annotation: `def create_user(...) -> UserPublic`. FastAPI checks the return value against `UserPublic`, **filters** it down to that model's fields, converts it to JSON (**serializes** it) and documents the response's shape.

Filtering is the important part. A common pattern is one model per direction:

- `UserCreate`: what the caller sends (includes `password`).
- `UserPublic`: what the caller sees (no secrets).
- `UserInDB`: what you store (includes `hashed_password`, a scrambled form of the password that can be checked but not reversed).

Inherit them from a shared base to avoid repetition. If the function returns a `UserInDB` but is annotated `-> UserPublic`, `hashed_password` is dropped from the response.

When the annotation would be wrong for the type checker, for example you return a dict but want the model in the docs, put it on the decorator instead: `@app.get("/users/{id}", response_model=UserPublic)`. `response_model` takes priority over the annotation, and `response_model=None` turns the feature off. `response_model_exclude_unset=True` leaves out fields that were never set, which keeps responses with many optional fields compact.

Set the success status code on the decorator: `status_code=201` ("created") when creating, `204` ("no content") for an empty "deleted" response. The constants in `fastapi.status` (`status.HTTP_201_CREATED`) read better than bare numbers.

If your return value doesn't fit the response model, that's a bug on the server side, so FastAPI raises an error and the caller gets a 500 ("internal server error"), not a 422. It's a useful safety net: a broken query can't silently ship malformed data.
takeaways: A return annotation or response_model checks, filters and documents the output
Use separate input, output and storage models so secrets never leave the server
response_model= on the decorator wins over the return annotation
Set success codes with status_code=, e.g. 201 for creation
pitfalls: Using the same model for input and output, so callers can set server-owned fields like id or see internal ones.

quiz.q: The function is annotated -> UserPublic but returns a UserInDB that has hashed_password. What does the client receive?
quiz.explain: FastAPI serializes using the declared response model, which filters out extra fields.

quiz.q: Your path operation returns a value that doesn't match its response model. What does the caller get?
options: A 500, because it's a server-side bug
quiz.explain: A response that fails its own check is the server's fault, so FastAPI answers with an internal server error.

concepts.name: Validation with Annotated, Query, Path and Field
concepts.summary: Add rules like max_length, ge/le and text patterns to parameters and model fields with Annotated.
concepts.why: Rejecting bad input at the door, with clear 422 errors and documented limits, beats hand-written checks in every function.
concepts.body:
Type hints say what type a value is; rules say which values are acceptable. The modern FastAPI style attaches rules with **`typing.Annotated`**: `q: Annotated[str | None, Query(max_length=50)] = None`. The first argument is the real type, the rest is extra information FastAPI reads, and the default stays an ordinary Python default.

The parameter functions say where a value comes from and carry its rules:

- `Query()`, `Path()`, `Header()` (an extra `Name: value` line sent with the request), `Cookie()` for parameters, `Body()` for extra values in the body.
- Strings: `min_length`, `max_length`, `pattern` (a **regular expression**, a mini-language for describing text patterns such as "two lowercase letters").
- Numbers: `gt`, `ge`, `lt`, `le` (greater than, at least, less than, at most), `multiple_of`.
- Documentation and naming: `title`, `description`, `examples`, `alias` (accept `item-query` in the URL), `deprecated=True`.

Inside Pydantic models, `Field()` takes the same rule names: `price: float = Field(gt=0)`. For rules that need code, write a **`@field_validator`** method for one field, or a `@model_validator(mode="after")` for rules across fields like "end must be after start". Raise `ValueError` with a clear message and Pydantic turns it into a 422 entry for the caller.

Since FastAPI 0.115 you can group query parameters into a model: `filters: Annotated[FilterParams, Query()]`. It's a neat way to share paging or search parameters, and with `model_config = {"extra": "forbid"}` unknown query keys are rejected.

Prefer `Annotated` over the older `q: str = Query(None, max_length=50)` form. Both work, but `Annotated` keeps defaults honest, lets the function be called normally in tests, and allows reusable aliases such as `ItemId = Annotated[int, Path(gt=0)]` shared across many path operations.
takeaways: Annotated[type, Query(...)/Path(...)/Body(...)] attaches rules and docs
Field() puts the same rules on model fields
field_validator and model_validator handle rules that need code; raise ValueError
Reusable aliases like ItemId = Annotated[int, Path(gt=0)] keep path operations consistent
pitfalls: Checking values inside the function and returning 400 by hand, so the rule never shows up in the docs or the standard 422 format.

quiz.q: Which is the recommended way to limit an optional query parameter q to 50 characters?
quiz.explain: Annotated carries the Query rules while the default stays a plain Python default.

quiz.q: A body model needs the rule 'end_date must be after start_date'. What's the best tool?
options: A check in a separate function run before every request
quiz.explain: Rules across fields belong in a model validator, which reports them as normal 422 errors.

concepts.name: Errors: HTTPException and exception handlers
concepts.summary: Raise HTTPException for expected failures, and register exception handlers that turn your own exceptions into responses.
concepts.why: Callers need consistent, meaningful error responses, and handlers keep HTTP details out of your core code.
concepts.body:
To stop a request with an error, **raise** `HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")`. Raise it rather than return it: it travels up through helper functions and dependencies, and FastAPI turns it into a JSON response `{"detail": "Item not found"}` with that status. `detail` can be any value JSON can hold, and `headers={...}` adds response headers.

Pick codes by meaning: 400 for a bad request the automatic checks couldn't catch, 401 when the caller hasn't proved who they are, 403 when they have but aren't allowed, 404 for something missing, 409 for a conflict such as a duplicate email. FastAPI already sends 422 for validation failures, and any exception you don't handle becomes a 500, with the stack trace written to the server's **log** (its running record of what happened, for you to read later).

Don't scatter HTTP details through the code that does the real work, though. Define your own exceptions (`class OutOfStock(Exception)`) and register an **exception handler** with `@app.exception_handler(OutOfStock)`. The handler receives the request and the exception and returns a response, usually a `JSONResponse`. Now any code that raises `OutOfStock` during a request, however deep, produces that response. Handlers match by class including subclasses, so one handler for a base `AppError` can cover a whole family.

You can also replace the built-in handlers:

- A handler for `RequestValidationError` changes the format of 422 responses; `exc.errors()` gives the error list.
- A handler for `starlette.exceptions.HTTPException` catches both your `HTTPException`s and Starlette's own 404 and 405 responses.
- To keep the default behaviour but add a log line, call `fastapi.exception_handlers.http_exception_handler` from your handler.

Keep error bodies consistent across the API; callers write their error handling once.
takeaways: raise HTTPException(status_code, detail) stops the request from any depth
401 = hasn't proved who they are, 403 = not allowed, 404 = missing, 409 = conflict
Map domain exceptions to responses with @app.exception_handler
Override RequestValidationError's handler to change the 422 format
pitfalls: Returning HTTPException instead of raising it: FastAPI then tries to turn the exception object itself into JSON.

quiz.q: Why is raising HTTPException better than returning an error dict from a helper function?
options: Raising stops execution from any depth, including helpers and dependencies, and FastAPI builds the error response
Returned dicts can't have a status code
quiz.explain: The exception travels up through every calling function, so callers don't have to check return values.

quiz.q: You register a handler for RequestValidationError. What changes?
options: Pydantic stops raising errors in your own code
The response sent when request data fails validation
quiz.explain: That handler produces the response for invalid requests, normally the standard 422.

concepts.name: Dependency injection with Depends
concepts.summary: Declare shared logic such as login checks, paging or database connections as functions, and let FastAPI call them and pass in the results.
concepts.why: Dependencies are FastAPI's main tool for reuse and for swapping parts out in tests, and they keep path operations thin.
concepts.body:
Many path operations need the same things first: the current user, paging settings, a database connection. In FastAPI, a **dependency** is any callable whose result your function needs. Declare it with `Depends`: `page: Annotated[dict, Depends(pagination)]`. For each request FastAPI calls `pagination` first, supplying whatever *it* declares (query parameters, headers, other dependencies), and passes the return value in. Your function never calls it and doesn't care where the values came from.

Dependencies use the full parameter system: their inputs are checked, they appear in the docs, and they can raise `HTTPException` to stop the request. That's exactly how login checks are built.

The usual pattern is a reusable alias for the whole annotation:

```python
CurrentUser = Annotated[User, Depends(get_current_user)]

def read_me(user: CurrentUser): ...
```

Things worth knowing:

- **Sub-dependencies**: a dependency can itself declare dependencies, and FastAPI works through the whole chain.
- **Once per request**: if several dependencies need the same one, it runs once and the value is shared. `Depends(fn, use_cache=False)` opts out.
- **Classes work** because they're callable: `Depends(Pagination)` builds an instance from query parameters.
- **Checks only**: `dependencies=[Depends(verify_key)]` on a decorator runs a check without passing anything in. `APIRouter(...)` and `FastAPI(...)` accept `dependencies=` too, applying them to every path operation.
- `def` and `async def` dependencies mix freely.

Dependencies are also how you swap parts out for tests: `app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = fake_db` replaces a dependency without touching the functions that use it.
takeaways: Annotated[T, Depends(fn)] runs fn for each request and passes in its result
Dependencies take parameters and other dependencies, forming a chain
A dependency used several times in one request runs once
dependencies=[...] on a path operation, a group of them or the app runs checks without passing values in
pitfalls: Calling the dependency yourself (Depends(get_db())) instead of passing the function (Depends(get_db)).

quiz.q: Two dependencies in one request both depend on get_settings. How many times does get_settings run?
options: Zero, only direct dependencies of the endpoint run
Once; its value is cached for the rest of the request
quiz.explain: FastAPI remembers each dependency's result for the rest of the request unless use_cache=False.

quiz.q: You need a dependency that only verifies an API key and returns nothing useful. What's the cleanest declaration?
options: Calling verify_key() at the top of each function
dependencies=[Depends(verify_key)] on the decorator, router or app
There is no other option than a check inside each function
quiz.explain: The dependencies list runs the callable without passing its value to the function.

concepts.name: APIRouter and project structure
concepts.summary: Split a growing app into one APIRouter per feature, and include them with prefixes, tags and shared dependencies.
concepts.why: A single main.py stops working after a few dozen path operations; routers give you modules a team can work in.
concepts.body:
An **`APIRouter`** is a mini-app: it has the same `.get`, `.post` and other decorators, and is attached to the real app with `app.include_router(router)`. Give each feature its own module and router:

```text
app/
  main.py          # creates FastAPI(), includes routers
  dependencies.py  # get_session, get_current_user...
  models.py        # Pydantic / SQLModel models
  routers/
    items.py
    users.py
```

A router can carry settings for all its path operations: `APIRouter(prefix="/items", tags=["items"], dependencies=[Depends(get_current_user)], responses={404: {"description": "Not found"}})`. Inside it, paths are relative: `@router.get("/{item_id}")` serves `/items/{item_id}`.

The same options can be passed when including instead: `app.include_router(admin.router, prefix="/admin", dependencies=[Depends(require_admin)])`. That's handy when you include a router you don't own, or attach one router under two prefixes. Settings combine: prefixes are joined, and tags and dependencies add up from app to router to path operation.

Routers can include other routers, so versioning an API is just a `v1 = APIRouter(prefix="/v1")` that includes the feature routers, and the app includes `v1`.

Two habits keep larger codebases healthy. Keep imports flowing one way: routers import from `dependencies.py` and `models.py`, and `main.py` imports the routers. If two modules end up importing each other (a circular import, which fails with `ImportError`), shared code lives in the wrong module. And keep path operation functions thin: read the input, call a plain function that does the work, return a model. Plain functions can be tested without HTTP at all.
takeaways: APIRouter has the same decorators as the app; attach it with app.include_router
prefix, tags and dependencies can be set on the router or when including it
Prefixes are joined and dependencies add up down the tree
One router per feature module; keep imports flowing one way
pitfalls: Ending a prefix with a slash (prefix='/items/') and getting paths like /items//{id}.

quiz.q: router = APIRouter(prefix='/users') with @router.get('/{id}') is included with app.include_router(router, prefix='/v1'). What's the final path?
quiz.explain: The prefix given at include time goes in front of the router's own prefix.

quiz.q: Where should a dependency that protects every admin route be declared?
options: On each admin path operation, so it's explicit
Once, on the admin router or in its include_router call
In a function that runs before every request of the whole app
At startup, before the app begins serving
quiz.explain: Router-level dependencies apply to every path operation in the router and can't be forgotten on a new one.

concepts.name: Settings with pydantic-settings
concepts.summary: Load configuration from environment variables and .env files into a typed, checked Settings class.
concepts.why: The same code runs on your laptop and in production with different settings, and a bad setting should fail at startup, not in the middle of a request.
concepts.body:
Database addresses and **secrets** (passwords, keys) written into the code are a classic production incident. Keep them outside the code, in **environment variables**: named values the operating system hands to a program when it starts (`DATABASE_URL=... fastapi run`). During development they usually live in a **`.env` file**, one `NAME=value` per line, that is never committed.

The standard FastAPI answer for reading them is **pydantic-settings**, a separate package since Pydantic v2 (`pip install pydantic-settings`; `fastapi[standard]` doesn't include it). Subclass `BaseSettings` and declare typed fields with defaults:

- Each field is read from an environment variable of the same name, ignoring letter case: `database_url` comes from `DATABASE_URL`.
- Values are checked and converted like any model: `debug: bool` accepts `1` or `true`, and `allowed_origins: list[str]` reads a JSON list written as text, such as `["https://a.com"]`.
- `model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", env_prefix="APP_")` also reads a `.env` file, and the prefix means every variable name starts with `APP_`, keeping them apart from other programs'. Real environment variables win over the file.
- Fields without defaults are required. A missing `APP_SECRET_KEY` raises a validation error the moment `Settings()` is created, so the app fails at startup instead of at the first log-in.
- `SecretStr` prints as `**********` in logs and error messages; call `.get_secret_value()` when you really need it.

Hand settings out through a dependency wrapped in `functools.lru_cache`, so the environment and `.env` file are read once rather than on every request:

```python
@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()
```

Path operations take `settings: Annotated[Settings, Depends(get_settings)]`, and tests swap values with `app.dependency_overrides[get_settings] = lambda: Settings(debug=True, secret_key="test")`. A module-level `settings = Settings()` also works and is common; the dependency version is easier to override and doesn't read the environment while the module is being imported.

Never commit `.env`. Commit a `.env.example` that lists every variable with a dummy value.
takeaways: BaseSettings fields come from environment variables (and optionally a .env file)
Values are checked; required fields without values fail at startup
Hand out settings via an lru_cache'd dependency so tests can override them
Use SecretStr for secrets and never commit .env
pitfalls: Forgetting that pydantic-settings is a separate install; BaseSettings no longer lives in pydantic itself.

quiz.q: Settings has secret_key: str with no default and the variable isn't set. When does it fail?
options: Never; it defaults to an empty string
At the first request that reads it
When Settings() is instantiated, with a validation error
quiz.explain: Missing required fields fail the check as soon as the settings object is created.

quiz.q: Why wrap get_settings in @lru_cache?
options: So the settings are created, and the environment read, once instead of on every request
To encrypt secret values in memory
quiz.explain: Without the cache, every request would rebuild Settings and re-read the .env file.

concepts.name: Databases with SQLModel
concepts.summary: Define tables as SQLModel classes, get a database session per request through a dependency, and create, read, update and delete rows.
concepts.why: Most APIs are a thin layer over a database; getting sessions and models right avoids leaked connections and exposed data.
concepts.body:
FastAPI has no built-in database layer; you bring one. **SQLModel**, by FastAPI's author, fits most directly: one class can be both a Pydantic model and a table definition, so a single declaration gives you validation and storage. It is built on **SQLAlchemy**, Python's most widely used SQL library. Plain SQLAlchemy with separate Pydantic models is equally common, and the session pattern is the same.

The moving parts:

- `create_engine(url)` once, when the app starts. The **engine** knows how to reach the database and keeps a few open connections ready for reuse (a connection pool), because opening a new one for every request is slow. For SQLite with plain `def` path operations add `connect_args={"check_same_thread": False}`, because FastAPI runs those on several threads at once.
- `SQLModel.metadata.create_all(engine)` creates the tables in demos; real projects use **Alembic**, the migration tool for SQLAlchemy, to change tables that already hold data.
- A **session dependency** that opens a `Session`, yields it to the path operation, and closes it when the request is done. A session tracks the rows you load and change and writes them in one transaction when you commit. The `yield` makes this a dependency with clean-up code; the Advanced level explains exactly when that clean-up runs.

Queries are built in Python: `session.exec(select(Hero).where(Hero.age > 30).limit(10)).all()`, `session.get(Hero, hero_id)` to fetch by primary key, and `session.add(obj)`, `session.commit()`, `session.refresh(obj)` to insert and then load values the database generated, such as the id.

Keep the separate-models discipline from the response models lesson. `table=True` marks the table class; `HeroCreate` and `HeroPublic` are plain Pydantic models for input and output, so callers can't set `id` and never see columns like `secret_name`. `Hero.model_validate(data)` turns checked input into a table row.

SQLModel and SQLAlchemy send your values separately from the SQL text, so an attacker can't smuggle SQL commands in through a field; never build SQL strings from request data with f-strings. And when a lookup finds nothing, raise a 404 rather than returning `None`.
takeaways: One engine per process; one session per request via a yield dependency
table=True models map to tables; separate Create/Public models shape the API
add + commit + refresh to insert and read back generated ids
Use Alembic for schema changes in real projects
pitfalls: Creating a new engine per request, which throws away the reusable connections.
Returning table objects without a response model and exposing internal columns.

quiz.q: Why does get_session use yield instead of return?
options: So the code after yield, closing the session, runs once the request has been handled
So one session is shared by all requests
quiz.explain: A yield dependency runs its setup before the path operation and its clean-up afterwards, like a context manager.

quiz.q: Why have HeroCreate and HeroPublic instead of using the Hero table class everywhere?
options: SQLModel table classes can't be used as parameters
So clients can't set server-owned fields like id or see columns like secret_name
Table classes are slower to serialize
quiz.explain: Separate input and output models define exactly what the API accepts and exposes.

concepts.name: Authentication: OAuth2 password flow and JWT
concepts.summary: Issue signed JWT tokens from a /token path operation and protect routes with an OAuth2PasswordBearer dependency.
concepts.why: Almost every API needs to know who is calling, and this is FastAPI's documented pattern, wired into /docs.
concepts.body:
Most APIs must know who is calling: proving who you are is **authentication**. FastAPI's security helpers are dependencies that also describe themselves in OpenAPI, so `/docs` gets an Authorize button. The common setup is the **OAuth2 password flow**: the caller logs in once with a username and password, receives a **token** (a string that proves who they are), and sends that token with every later request.

- The caller POSTs form fields `username` and `password` to `/token`; `OAuth2PasswordRequestForm` reads them (reading form fields needs `python-multipart`, included in `fastapi[standard]`).
- You check the password against a stored **hash** (a scrambled form that can be checked but not reversed), never against the password itself. FastAPI's docs use `pwdlib` with the Argon2 method via `PasswordHash.recommended()`.
- You return `{"access_token": token, "token_type": "bearer"}`. The token is a **JWT** (JSON Web Token): a small JSON document, such as `{"sub": "ann", "exp": ...}`, **signed** with a server secret so any change to it is detected. The PyJWT library builds and checks them.
- Later requests send the header `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")` is a dependency that extracts the token, or answers 401 if it's missing.
- Your `current_user` dependency decodes it (`jwt.decode` checks the signature and the `exp` expiry), loads the user, and raises 401 with the header `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer` on any failure.

Path operations then just declare `user: Annotated[User, Depends(current_user)]`. Layer extra checks as further dependencies: one that rejects disabled accounts, another that requires an admin role.

A JWT is **signed, not encrypted** (scrambled so only key holders can read it): anyone holding it can read its contents, so put only identifiers in it. Keep tokens short-lived (15 to 60 minutes), keep the secret in settings, and always pass `algorithms=[...]` to `decode` so a forged token can't pick its own signing method. Send tokens only over HTTPS (encrypted HTTP). If users sign in through Google or a company log-in service, you check that service's tokens instead, but the dependency shape stays the same.
takeaways: /token checks a password hash and returns a signed, expiring JWT
OAuth2PasswordBearer pulls the bearer token from the Authorization header
A current_user dependency checks the token; path operations just depend on it
JWTs are readable by anyone: sign them, expire them and keep secrets out of them
pitfalls: Calling jwt.decode without algorithms=[...], or with the checks turned off.
Storing passwords as plain text or with fast hash methods (MD5, SHA-256) instead of Argon2 or bcrypt.

quiz.q: Why must jwt.decode be given algorithms=['HS256']?
options: So the server, not the token header, decides which algorithm is acceptable
PyJWT can't detect the algorithm otherwise
quiz.explain: Fixing the method blocks attacks where a forged token names a weaker or different signing method.

quiz.q: A request to a route protected by OAuth2PasswordBearer has no Authorization header. What happens?
options: The token parameter is None and the function runs
FastAPI responds 401 Not authenticated before the function runs
FastAPI calls /token on the caller's behalf
quiz.explain: The scheme dependency itself rejects requests without a bearer token.

concepts.name: Middleware and CORS
concepts.summary: Run code around every request with middleware, and let web pages on other sites call your API with CORSMiddleware.
concepts.why: Timing headers, request ids and CORS apply to every request, so they belong in one place rather than in every function.
concepts.body:
**Middleware** wraps the whole application: it sees every request before any path operation runs and every response before it leaves. The quickest form is a decorator:

```python
@app.middleware("http")
async def add_timing(request: Request, call_next):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["X-Process-Time"] = f"{time.perf_counter() - start:.4f}"
    return response
```

`call_next` passes the request on to the rest of the app and returns the response. Middleware added later wraps the earlier ones, so the **last one added runs first** on the way in. Keep middleware for truly global concerns: request ids, timing, security headers, `GZipMiddleware` (compresses responses). Per-route logic belongs in dependencies, which see checked parameters and appear in the docs.

**CORS** (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the middleware almost everyone needs. Browsers group sites by **origin**: the start of a web address, made of three parts. The scheme is `https` or `http`, the host is the site's name, and the port is the numbered door on that server (443 is assumed for https when none is written). So `https://app.example.com` is one origin and `https://api.example.com` is another.

Web pages can contain JavaScript, the programming language browsers run inside pages. Code on a page from one origin may send a request to another, say `https://api.example.com`, but the browser won't let the page read the response unless the API answers with matching `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers. For requests with JSON bodies, custom headers or methods like PUT and DELETE, the browser first sends an `OPTIONS` request on its own, a **preflight**, asking whether the real request is allowed. `CORSMiddleware` handles all of it:

- `allow_origins`: exact origins, scheme + host + port, no path or trailing slash.
- `allow_credentials=True` if the browser sends cookies (small pieces of data a site stores in the browser, such as who is logged in) or Authorization headers. The CORS rules forbid the wildcard `*` origin together with credentials, so list origins one by one.
- `allow_methods` and `allow_headers` allow very little by default; `["*"]` is common.

CORS is a browser rule, not protection for your API: curl, scripts and other servers ignore it entirely. Authentication still has to guard your path operations.
concepts.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

app = FastAPI()
app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://app.example.com", "http://localhost:5173"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"],
)

@app.get("/data")
def data():
    return {"ok": True}

c = TestClient(app)
pre = c.options("/data", headers={"Origin": "http://localhost:5173",
                                  "Access-Control-Request-Method": "GET"})
print(pre.status_code, pre.headers["access-control-allow-origin"])
# 200 http://localhost:5173
other = c.get("/data", headers={"Origin": "https://evil.example"})
print("access-control-allow-origin" in other.headers)
# False: the browser won't let that page read the response
takeaways: Middleware wraps every request; the last added runs first on the way in
Use middleware for global concerns, dependencies for per-route logic
CORSMiddleware answers preflights and adds Access-Control-Allow-* headers
CORS only restricts browsers; it is not authentication
pitfalls: Adding a trailing slash or path to an origin (https://app.example.com/), which never matches.

quiz.q: Your web page on http://localhost:5173 gets a CORS error calling your API, but the same request works with curl. Why?
options: The API only accepts curl's user agent
CORS is enforced by the browser, and the API isn't sending Access-Control-Allow-Origin for that origin
quiz.explain: Only browsers apply CORS; add the web page's origin to CORSMiddleware.

quiz.q: You call app.add_middleware(A) and then app.add_middleware(B). Which sees the request first?
quiz.explain: Each add_middleware wraps the existing ones, so the last one added is outermost.

concepts.name: Background tasks
concepts.summary: Schedule small jobs, like sending an email, to run after the response is sent, using the BackgroundTasks parameter.
concepts.why: Users shouldn't wait for a notification email or a log entry to be written before they get their response.
concepts.body:
Some work doesn't need to finish before the caller gets an answer: sending a welcome email, writing an entry to an **audit log** (a permanent record of who did what, when). Declare a parameter of type **`BackgroundTasks`** and FastAPI passes in an instance. Call `background_tasks.add_task(func, *args, **kwargs)` and return as usual: the response goes out first, then the tasks run in the order they were added, inside the same running program. `func` can be a plain `def` (run on a separate thread) or an `async def`.

`BackgroundTasks` also works in dependencies. A dependency can declare it and add tasks, and FastAPI merges everything into one list for the request, which suits things like "write an access log entry" inside a log-in dependency.

Know the limits, because this is a convenience, not a job queue:

- Tasks exist only in the program's memory. If the server restarts or crashes, pending tasks are lost, and nothing tries them again.
- They run in the same server **worker** (one of the copies of your app handling requests) that answered the request, and share its resources. A heavy task slows that worker, and a slow call that doesn't use `await` inside an `async` task stalls everything else that worker is doing.
- The caller never learns whether a task succeeded; exceptions are only written to the log.

So use them for short, best-effort side effects: a notification, an audit record, clearing a cached value. For work that must happen, takes minutes, needs to be retried on failure or should run on other machines, use a real **task queue**: a separate system (Celery, RQ, Dramatiq, Arq or a cloud provider's queue) that stores jobs until separate worker programs pick them up. The path operation adds a job and returns its id, often with status 202 ("accepted").

Pass tasks plain values such as an email address or a row id, not objects that belong to the request, like the database session from a dependency, which is closed once the request ends. Open whatever the task needs, such as a fresh session, inside the task itself.
takeaways: Add a BackgroundTasks parameter and call add_task(func, *args)
Tasks run after the response is sent, in the same program
Dependencies can add tasks too; they're merged per request
Use a real task queue for anything that must not be lost or needs retries
pitfalls: Passing the request's database session to a task instead of opening a new one inside it.

quiz.q: Your server restarts while 50 background tasks are still pending. What happens to them?
options: FastAPI saves them to disk first
They're lost, because BackgroundTasks keeps them in memory
quiz.explain: BackgroundTasks keeps nothing on disk and never retries; use a task queue when that matters.

quiz.q: When do tasks added with add_task run?
options: At the same time as the path operation function
After the response has been sent
At the start of the next request
quiz.explain: FastAPI sends the response first and then runs the tasks in order.

concepts.name: Testing with TestClient and pytest
concepts.summary: Call your app directly with TestClient, swap dependencies with dependency_overrides, and check the responses.
concepts.why: Fast, reliable API tests catch breakage in validation, log-in checks and response shapes before users do.
concepts.body:
**`TestClient`** (from `fastapi.testclient`, built on the HTTPX library) sends requests straight into your app with no server or network. It has the familiar `client.get`, `.post(json=...)`, `.put`, `.delete` methods, and each returns a response with `.status_code`, `.json()` and `.headers`. Tests are ordinary pytest functions without `async`, even when your path operations are `async def`.

Use it in a `with` block, `with TestClient(app) as client:`, when your app has a **lifespan** function (code that runs once at startup and once at shutdown; a later lesson). Entering the block runs startup and leaving runs shutdown. Without `with`, the lifespan never runs, and anything it creates is missing.

The real power is `app.dependency_overrides`, a dict that maps an original dependency to a replacement. Override `get_session` to use a test database, `current_user` to skip logging in, `get_settings` to switch a feature on. Overrides are looked up on every request, so set them in a fixture and clear them afterwards with `app.dependency_overrides.clear()`; otherwise they leak into other tests.

What's worth testing:

- the normal case and the exact response shape (`assert r.json() == {...}`),
- validation: bad input returns 422,
- log-in checks: no token gives 401, the wrong role 403,
- errors: missing things give 404, and your exception handlers produce their format,
- the docs: `client.get("/openapi.json")` returns 200, which catches models that can't be described.

For a test database, SQLite in a temporary file or a throwaway PostgreSQL server both work; the override pattern is the same. When a test itself must `await` things, such as async database setup, use `httpx.AsyncClient(transport=httpx.ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://test")` together with a pytest add-on that runs async tests, such as AnyIO's.
takeaways: TestClient calls the app directly; tests stay ordinary functions
Use `with TestClient(app)` so lifespan startup and shutdown run
app.dependency_overrides swaps dependencies; clear it after each test
Test the error paths (401, 404, 422) as well as the normal case
pitfalls: Leaving dependency overrides in place between tests, so later tests pass or fail for the wrong reason.

quiz.q: Your app opens a set of database connections in its lifespan, and tests fail with 'pool not initialized'. What's the likely fix?
options: Use `with TestClient(app) as client:` so lifespan startup runs
Call app.startup() at the top of each test
Start Uvicorn in a separate process
quiz.explain: TestClient only runs the lifespan when used in a with block.

quiz.q: How do you make every request in a test act as user 'ann' without real tokens?
quiz.explain: Overriding the dependency replaces the whole log-in check for the test.

concepts.name: async def vs def and the threadpool
concepts.summary: How FastAPI runs async def functions on the event loop and plain def ones in a threadpool, and how to choose between them.
concepts.why: Choosing wrong can silently make a whole worker handle one request at a time; it's the most common FastAPI performance bug.
concepts.body:
A production server runs several copies of your app, each a separate **worker** process. Each worker runs one event loop (via Starlette and the AnyIO library). What happens to your function depends on how you declare it:

- `async def` runs **on the event loop**. While it waits at an `await`, the loop serves other requests. But a blocking call inside it, such as `time.sleep`, `requests.get`, a database **driver** (the library that talks to the database) without async support, or heavy computation, freezes the loop, and every request on that worker waits.
- Plain `def` runs in a **threadpool** via `run_in_threadpool`, so blocking I/O only ties up one thread. The same rules apply to dependencies.

The decision rule:

- The code awaits async libraries (`httpx.AsyncClient`, asyncpg, SQLAlchemy's asyncio extension, `redis.asyncio`): use `async def`.
- The code calls blocking libraries: use `def`.
- Trivial code with no I/O: either works, and `async def` skips the hop to a thread.

The threadpool is AnyIO's default limit of **40 threads** per worker. Under load with slow blocking calls, requests wait in line for a free thread even though the CPU is idle. You can raise the limit at startup (`anyio.to_thread.current_default_thread_limiter().total_tokens = 100`), but threads cost memory and get in each other's way; moving your busiest code to async drivers usually scales further.

When an async function must call one blocking function, push it off the loop with `await run_in_threadpool(fn, arg)` from `fastapi.concurrency`, or `await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(fn, arg)`. CPU-heavy work such as image processing doesn't belong in the web process at all: Python threads don't execute Python code in parallel (the GIL, a lock in the standard interpreter, lets one thread run at a time), so use a pool of separate processes or a task queue.

A quick check: if `/health` gets slow whenever one heavy path operation is busy, something is blocking the event loop.
concepts.code:
import asyncio, time
import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/bad")
async def bad():
    time.sleep(0.5)            # blocks the event loop
    return "bad"

@app.get("/sync")
def sync():
    time.sleep(0.5)            # runs in the threadpool
    return "ok"

@app.get("/async")
async def non_blocking():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)   # yields to the loop while waiting
    return "ok"

async def main():
    transport = httpx.ASGITransport(app=app)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(transport=transport, base_url="http://t") as c:
        for path in ("/bad", "/sync", "/async"):
            start = time.perf_counter()
            await asyncio.gather(*(c.get(path) for _ in range(5)))
            print(path, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 1))

asyncio.run(main())   # /bad 2.5   /sync 0.5   /async 0.5
takeaways: async def runs on the event loop: never block inside it
def runs in a 40-thread pool: safe for blocking libraries
Use run_in_threadpool to call one blocking function from async code
CPU-bound work belongs in separate processes or a task queue, not the web worker
pitfalls: Calling requests, time.sleep or a blocking database driver inside async def.
Making everything async def 'for speed' while still using blocking libraries.

quiz.q: An async def path operation calls requests.get(), which takes 2 s. Ten requests arrive at once on one worker. What happens?
options: All finish in about 2 s because the endpoint is async
FastAPI detects the blocking call and moves it to a thread
They run one after another, about 20 s in total, because the event loop is blocked
The requests fail with a timeout error immediately
quiz.explain: A blocking call inside async def holds the loop, so the other requests can't progress.

quiz.q: What's the smallest correct fix for that path operation?
options: Change it to a plain def so it runs in the threadpool
quiz.explain: A def function runs on a threadpool thread, where blocking only occupies that thread.

concepts.name: Dependencies with yield and scopes
concepts.summary: Use yield in dependencies for setup and teardown, handle exceptions in them, and control when teardown runs with scope.
concepts.why: Database sessions, transactions, locks and open files need reliable clean-up, including when the path operation raises.
concepts.body:
A dependency that **yields** works like a context manager: code before `yield` is setup, the yielded value is passed in, and code after `yield` is teardown (clean-up). FastAPI wraps it with `contextlib.contextmanager` (or `asynccontextmanager` for `async def`) and keeps them on a stack, so teardowns run in reverse order of setup. Plain `def` generator dependencies run both halves in the threadpool.

Exceptions flow into the dependency: if the path operation or a later dependency raises, the exception is re-raised at the `yield`. That enables a transaction pattern:

```python
def get_tx_session():
    with Session(engine) as session:
        try:
            yield session
            session.commit()
        except Exception:
            session.rollback()
            raise
```

Always re-raise in an `except` block, or raise a new `HTTPException`. If you swallow the exception, the caller still gets a 500 but nothing is written to the log, which makes the bug very hard to find. Raising `HTTPException` *before* the `yield` is fine too, for example when a lock can't be acquired.

**When** does teardown run? Since FastAPI 0.118 the default, `scope="request"`, runs it after the response has been sent, so the resource stays alive while a `StreamingResponse` sends its body piece by piece (see the streaming lesson). (From 0.106 to 0.117 it ran before sending.) The catch: a commit after `yield` happens after the caller already received its 200, so a failing commit can't change the response. Two fixes:

- commit explicitly in the path operation before returning, or
- since 0.121, declare `Depends(get_tx_session, scope="function")`, which runs teardown as soon as the path operation function returns, before the response is sent.

A `"function"`-scoped dependency may depend on `"request"`-scoped ones but not the reverse, because outer resources must outlive inner ones.
takeaways: Code before yield is setup, after yield is teardown, in reverse order
Exceptions from the path operation are re-raised at the yield: always re-raise
Default scope='request' tears down after the response is sent (0.118+)
scope='function' (0.121+) tears down before the response, so commit errors can still fail the request
pitfalls: Catching an exception after yield and not re-raising it, which hides the error from the logs.

quiz.q: With the default scope, a dependency commits after yield and the commit fails. What has the caller already received?
options: Nothing; the response waits for the commit
The successful response, because teardown runs after it was sent
quiz.explain: Request-scoped teardown runs after sending, so its errors can't change the response.

quiz.q: Which dependency arrangement is invalid?
options: A plain return-style dependency inside a yield dependency
A scope='function' dependency depending on a scope='request' one
Two scope='request' dependencies depending on each other in a chain
A scope='request' dependency depending on a scope='function' one
quiz.explain: A request-scoped resource outlives the function scope, so it can't rely on something already torn down.

concepts.name: Lifespan: startup and shutdown
concepts.summary: Create shared resources such as connection pools, HTTP clients or loaded ML models once per worker with a lifespan function.
concepts.why: Opening a client or loading a model for every request is slow and wastes resources; once-per-worker setup belongs in lifespan.
concepts.body:
Some things should exist once per worker process, not once per request: a database engine, an `httpx.AsyncClient` (a reusable client for calling other web services), a pool of connections to Redis (a fast in-memory database), a loaded machine-learning model. FastAPI's tool for this is **lifespan**: an async context manager passed to `FastAPI(lifespan=...)`. Code before its `yield` runs at startup, before the server accepts requests; code after it runs at shutdown, once requests have stopped.

Lifespan replaces the older, deprecated `@app.on_event("startup")` and `@app.on_event("shutdown")` handlers. Don't mix them: when you pass `lifespan`, `on_event` handlers aren't called.

Where to keep the resources? Module globals work, but **lifespan state** is cleaner: yield a dict, `yield {"http": client}`, and each request can read it as `request.state.http` (every request gets a shallow copy of that dict). Wrap the lookup in a dependency so path operations stay simple and tests can override it:

```python
def get_http(request: Request) -> httpx.AsyncClient:
    return request.state.http
```

Things to keep in mind:

- Each worker process runs its own lifespan. Four workers mean four pools, so size them accordingly.
- If startup raises, the server doesn't start. That's good: fail at once on bad configuration or an unreachable database.
- Only the main app's lifespan runs, not those of sub-applications mounted with `app.mount`.
- In tests, lifespan runs only inside `with TestClient(app) as client:`.

Clean up in reverse order of creation, and put the cleanup after `yield` in a `try/finally` if you open several resources, or use `contextlib.AsyncExitStack`.
concepts.code:
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from typing import Annotated
import httpx
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI, Request
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    client = httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5)
    print("startup: client created")
    yield {"http": client}          # becomes request.state.http
    await client.aclose()
    print("shutdown: client closed")

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

def get_http(request: Request) -> httpx.AsyncClient:
    return request.state.http

@app.get("/client")
async def which_client(http: Annotated[httpx.AsyncClient, Depends(get_http)]):
    return {"closed": http.is_closed}

with TestClient(app) as c:              # runs startup ... shutdown
    print(c.get("/client").json())      # {'closed': False}
takeaways: lifespan = async context manager: before yield is startup, after is shutdown
Yield a dict to expose resources as request.state.<name>
Each worker process runs its own lifespan
Use lifespan instead of the deprecated on_event handlers
pitfalls: Creating an httpx.AsyncClient or database engine inside each request instead of once in lifespan.

quiz.q: You run the app with 4 workers and the lifespan creates a pool of 10 database connections. How many connections can the app open?
options: 40, since each worker runs its own lifespan
quiz.explain: Workers are separate processes, each with its own lifespan and pool.

quiz.q: Where do resources yielded from lifespan as a dict show up?
options: As request.state attributes in each request
quiz.explain: Lifespan state is copied into each request's state.

concepts.name: Uploads, file and streaming responses
concepts.summary: Accept uploads with UploadFile, send files with FileResponse, and stream generated data with StreamingResponse.
concepts.why: Files, and large or slow-to-produce responses, would use up memory or run out of time if handled as one JSON value.
concepts.body:
**Uploads** arrive as a **multipart form**: the body format browsers use for forms with files, split into one part per field or file (read by `python-multipart`, part of `fastapi[standard]`). Declare `file: UploadFile` and you get `filename`, `content_type`, `size` and a temporary file that is kept in memory up to a size limit and then moved to disk, so large uploads don't fill your RAM. Read it with `await file.read(size)` in chunks, or use the plain `file.file` object. A `bytes` parameter (with `File()`) loads everything into memory, so keep it for small files.

Combine files with `Form()` fields, and use `list[UploadFile]` for several files. A multipart request can't also carry a JSON body, so extra information travels as form fields. `filename` and `content_type` come from the caller: never use the filename as a path on disk (a name like `../../app.py` could overwrite your code), and enforce size and type limits yourself.

**Sending files**: `FileResponse(path, media_type=..., filename="report.pdf")` sends the file from disk in chunks and sets `Content-Disposition` so browsers download it under that name.

**Streaming**: `StreamingResponse(iterator, media_type=...)` sends whatever a generator (plain or async) yields as soon as it's produced. That suits CSV exports, passing on a download from another server, or the words of an AI model's answer as they're generated. It skips response models, so you convert each chunk to text or bytes yourself.
